title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context: modulus p = 2n+1 prime, a primitive root, so the residues of 1, a, a^2, …, a^{2n-1} run through all nonzero classes, and a^{n+λ} ≡ −a^λ (Coroll. 41–42).

(i) End of Scholion 43. Two residues r, s are 'socii' (companions) when rs ≡ 1 (mod p), i.e. they are multiplicative inverses. If r ≡ a^{n+ν} and s ≡ a^{n−ν}, then rs ≡ a^{2n} ≡ 1. So in the cyclic listing, companions sit symmetrically about the middle term a^n ≡ −1. The only self-companions are +1 and −1; all other companion pairs consist of unequal residues. For any r coprime to p, its companion is s = (1 + m(2n+1))/r, where m is chosen so that r divides m(2n+1)+1. Such an m exists because p is prime and r < p (or at least gcd(r,p)=1). Euler remarks that the cyclic arrangement makes inverses easy to read off.

(ii) Theorem 44. For a prime P, the number of primitive roots in 1…P−1 equals the number of integers below Q = P−1 that are coprime to Q, i.e. φ(P−1).

Proof (begun here, finished on p.105). Assume one primitive root a exists, so ord(a) = Q. Take n with gcd(n,Q)=1 and let b ≡ a^n. Consider the progression 1, a^n, a^{2n}, …, a^{Qn}. Since a^k ≡ 1 only when Q | k, we have a^{mn} ≡ 1 only if Q | mn. That forces Q | m, so no term before a^{Qn} is ≡ 1. Hence ord(b) = Q and b is a primitive root. Each n coprime to Q therefore gives a primitive root, and the count follows.

In modern terms this is the standard fact that a cyclic group of order Q has exactly φ(Q) generators.
errors: The remark that b ≡ a^n 'will certainly differ from a' is false for n = 1. It is harmless, since n = 1 just returns a.

Two steps needed for the exact count are not stated explicitly. Distinct n < Q give distinct b, which follows from ord(a) = Q. Every primitive root equals a^k for some k with gcd(k,Q) = 1, because a^k with gcd(k,Q) = d > 1 has order Q/d. On this page and the next, the proof shows only that there are at least φ(Q) primitive roots.

The existence of a primitive root ('cum certe detur radix primitiua') is taken from Euler's earlier argument in this paper. Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, art. 56) judged that existence proof to be deficient. The theorem is therefore conditional on that earlier, flawed step.

ideas.what: Inverse residues are placed symmetrically about −1 in the power cycle of a primitive root; only ±1 are self-inverse; an explicit inverse formula s = (1+m p)/r is given.
ideas.modern_name: Modular inverse via discrete logarithm: ind(r^{-1}) = −ind(r); x^2 ≡ 1 mod p implies x ≡ ±1
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler; Lagrange/Wilson-theorem context; Gauss's index calculus
ideas.where_published: E449 (Novi Comm. 18) and Euler's earlier residue papers (E262 and related)

ideas.what: The number of primitive roots of a prime P is φ(P−1); a^n is primitive exactly when gcd(n, P−1) = 1.
ideas.modern_name: Number of generators of a cyclic group of order P−1 is φ(P−1)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449, 1774); stated by Lambert 1769; rigorously proved by Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 52–56)
ideas.where_published: E449, §44; discussed by Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae art. 56) and in standard histories (e.g. Weil, Number Theory: an approach through history)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known E449 statement and proof that there are φ(P−1) primitive roots. Gauss explicitly credits and critiques it, so nothing on the page is absent from the historical record.
